paragraphs: Deep equilibrium models represent computation by finding a fixed point of one layer, rather than passing inputs through a stack of distinct layers. This design offers memory efficiency, but it also complicates the evaluation of adversarial robustness: attacks need gradients that accurately reflect how the model produces its predictions.

The paper identifies two problems. Adversarial training can make the model require more forward steps to reach equilibrium, and can even disrupt its fixed-point structure. Meanwhile, the black-box solvers used by DEQs can make the forward computation and backward gradient calculation follow misaligned paths. Together, these effects can obscure gradients and undermine ready-made attacks used for evaluation or training.

The authors estimate gradients at intermediate stages and incorporate those estimates into attack pipelines. This supports white-box evaluations and more effective adversarial defense. Experiments on CIFAR-10 find robustness competitive with similarly sized deep networks. The contribution connects the reliability of robustness measurements to the numerical procedures that make equilibrium models work.
neurips-2022-a-closer-look-at-the-advers.tldr: Estimating intermediate gradients enables more reliable adversarial evaluation and training of deep equilibrium models.

paragraphs: A constrained Markov decision process describes learning to make decisions while respecting specified constraints. This paper studies the offline version, where learning must rely entirely on an existing dataset. Its central questions are how much data this requires and whether an algorithm can learn an effective policy without violating the constraints.

The authors establish a lower bound on the required number of samples using a single-policy concentrability coefficient, C*. The bound accounts for the numbers of states, actions, and constraints, as well as the discount factor and desired accuracy. This gives a theoretical reference for judging how close an algorithm comes to the best possible sample requirements in the studied setting.

They then introduce DPDL, a primal-dual algorithm with a deviation-control mechanism. It provably achieves zero constraint violation and matches the lower bound apart from an additional factor involving the discount factor, up to logarithmic terms. The paper also discusses handling unknown C* and possible asynchronous structure in the offline data.
neurips-2022-a-near-optimal-primal-dual-.tldr: DPDL learns constrained policies from offline data with zero constraint violation and sample requirements close to a proved lower bound.

paragraphs: In multiagent reinforcement learning, a population of different strategies can help against unfamiliar opponents. Diversity is especially useful when strategies form cycles of advantage, as in Rock-Paper-Scissors. However, competing definitions of diversity make it difficult to compare learning methods or explain which kinds of variation improve a strategy population.

The paper introduces the Unified Diversity Measure, or UDM, to provide a common perspective on existing diversity metrics. It then builds two learning algorithms around that measure: UDM-Fictitious Play for normal-form games and UDM-Policy Space Response Oracle for open-ended games. Diversity therefore becomes part of the procedure for developing the strategy pool, rather than only a quantity measured afterward.

The theoretical results show that UDM-based methods can expand the gamescape by increasing the pool's response capacity, and establish convergence guarantees to a two-player Nash equilibrium. On games with strong non-transitivity, the proposed algorithms outperform strong PSRO baselines on exploitability and population effectivity. These findings connect the diversity measure to both strategic coverage and observed competitive performance.
neurips-2022-a-unified-diversity-measure.tldr: A unified diversity measure supports strategy-population algorithms with theoretical guarantees and improved results on strongly non-transitive games.

paragraphs: Automatic differentiation constructs a program that computes derivatives of another program. Discrete randomness creates a difficulty: changing a coin's probability of heads does not produce a smoothly changing individual outcome. Yet the expected output of a program using that coin can change with the probability, making its derivative useful for optimization.

The paper develops a reparameterization-based method that generates programs whose expected output equals the derivative of the original program's expected output. The distinction matters: the method targets sensitivity of an expectation, rather than treating an individual discrete outcome as a continuously varying value. The authors present the resulting estimator as unbiased, low variance, and as automated as traditional automatic differentiation.

Demonstrations cover forward-mode differentiation of discrete-time Markov chains and agent-based models, including Conway's Game of Life, alongside reverse-mode differentiation of a particle filter. These examples show the method operating across several kinds of stochastic computation. The contribution extends automated derivative estimation to programs whose behavior includes parameter-dependent discrete random choices.
neurips-2022-automatic-differentiation-o.tldr: A reparameterization-based method automatically estimates derivatives of expected program outputs despite discrete random choices.

paragraphs: Research on neural-network backdoor attacks and defenses develops rapidly, but evaluating progress is difficult when implementations and experimental settings vary. The paper argues that incomplete comparisons make it hard to verify reported performance or understand how new methods relate to existing ones. BackdoorBench addresses this evaluation problem with shared infrastructure.

The benchmark combines an extensible, modular codebase with a standardized protocol for backdoor learning. Its reported implementation includes eight attack methods and nine defense methods. The evaluation covers attack-defense pairings across five poisoning ratios, five models, and four datasets, with the abstract reporting 8,000 evaluation pairs in total.

The authors analyze these evaluations from several perspectives to study how different factors affect backdoor learning. The contribution is therefore both a collection of implementations and a common experimental basis for comparing them. Publicly available code and evaluations support reproducibility and further investigation, while the modular design provides a way to incorporate additional methods as the research area develops.
neurips-2022-backdoorbench-a-comprehensi.tldr: BackdoorBench standardizes implementations and evaluations of backdoor attacks and defenses to make comparisons more reproducible.

paragraphs: Combining camera images with LiDAR point clouds is a common approach to detecting objects in three dimensions. The paper identifies a structural weakness in fusion methods that use LiDAR points to query image features: their ability to use the camera depends on receiving suitable LiDAR input. A malfunction can therefore prevent predictions despite the availability of images.

BEVFusion changes this dependency by giving the camera stream a way to operate without LiDAR input. This architectural choice addresses the failure pathway identified in the earlier fusion framework. The central idea is that combining sensors should preserve the camera stream's ability to contribute when the other sensor malfunctions.

Experiments show improvements over state-of-the-art methods under normal training settings. Under robustness training that simulates different LiDAR malfunctions, the authors report gains of 15.7% to 28.9% mAP over those methods. They also state that the framework can handle realistic malfunction scenarios without post-processing. These results support the value of sensor independence within the fusion design.
neurips-2022-bevfusion-a-simple-and-robu.tldr: BEVFusion makes its camera stream independent of LiDAR input, improving detection under normal settings and simulated LiDAR malfunctions.

paragraphs: Class-incremental semantic segmentation must learn to label pixels with new categories while retaining previously learned categories. Existing approaches often preserve old classifier scores through knowledge distillation or freeze the feature extractor. The paper argues that these constraints can interfere with learning features that distinguish new classes.

The authors decompose a class score, or logit, into two terms describing evidence for belonging and not belonging to that class. Preserving only their sum allows the individual terms to change, so matching the old score need not preserve the reasoning represented by those components. Decomposed knowledge distillation explicitly constrains each term to address forgetting more effectively.

The framework also introduces an initialization method for new classifiers. Because new classes lack enough negative training examples to distinguish them from old classes, an auxiliary classifier successively transfers knowledge about negatives. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. Together, the two mechanisms address what information should be retained and how newly added classifiers should acquire useful distinctions.
neurips-2022-decomposed-knowledge-distil.tldr: Preserving separate components of class scores and transferring negative-class knowledge improves incremental semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains across clients without centrally collecting their private datasets. Two complications are that clients hold differently distributed data and may leave the training process. DReS-FL addresses both problems through a coded data-sharing framework designed to preserve privacy while supporting collaborative gradient computation.

The method uses Lagrange coding to secretly share datasets among clients. Each client receives an encoded version of the global dataset, and its local gradient computation over that representation is unbiased. This gives local computation access to information representing the global data while using an encoded sharing mechanism to protect the original datasets.

Correctly decoding gradients at the server requires the gradient function to be polynomial over a finite field. The authors therefore construct polynomial integer neural networks to satisfy this requirement. Their theoretical analysis establishes dropout resilience and privacy protection for local datasets, and experiments show significant gains over baseline methods. The network design is a functional requirement of the coding approach, linking the learning model to the mathematical operations needed for secure computation.
neurips-2022-dres-fl-dropout-resilient-s.tldr: DReS-FL combines secretly shared coded data with polynomial integer neural networks to address heterogeneous clients and dropouts.

paragraphs: Transformer attention depends on similarities between queries and keys, but computing it can consume substantial energy and computation. Ordinary binarization methods compress numerical values without specifically preserving those pairwise relationships. EcoFormer designs the compression around attention's similarity structure so that reducing numerical precision also respects the operation being approximated.

The method learns kernelized hash functions that turn queries and keys into compact binary codes. Training uses similarity relationships extracted from the attention map as self-supervision. Relationships between binary inner products and Hamming distance, together with reassociation of matrix multiplication, allow attention to be approximated with linear complexity. Binary representations also replace many multiply-accumulate operations with simpler accumulations.

Experiments across vision and language tasks find performance comparable to standard attention with substantially fewer resources. For PVTv2-B0 on ImageNet-1K, the authors report a 73% reduction in on-chip energy footprint with a 0.33% performance drop. The result illustrates the intended tradeoff: preserve useful attention relationships while reducing the arithmetic and energy needed to process them.
neurips-2022-ecoformer-energy-saving-att.tldr: EcoFormer learns binary query and key representations that preserve attention similarities while reducing computational and energy costs.

paragraphs: Federated Averaging alternates several local learning updates at clients with model averaging at a server. Empirical studies have found that its resulting model can adapt well to unseen tasks after a few fine-tuning steps. This paper investigates why that can happen through a theoretical study of multi-task linear regression.

In the setting where tasks share an underlying linear representation, the authors show that FedAvg can learn that common representation. Multiple local updates between communication rounds allow it to use differences among client data distributions productively. The analysis also establishes the client iteration complexity required for this representation-learning result.

The role of multiple updates is especially consequential: in the studied linear setting, distributed gradient methods using only one local update per round cannot recover the ground-truth representation. Experiments on heterogeneous image-classification datasets likewise find substantially worse transfer to new clients from single-update neural-network representations. The formal necessity claim belongs to the linear setting, while the image results provide empirical evidence of a related distinction.
neurips-2022-fedavg-with-fine-tuning-loc.tldr: In a shared linear-representation setting, multiple local FedAvg updates enable representation learning that helps explain adaptation to new tasks.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds seek to connect a model's training procedure to its performance beyond the training data. Existing analyses of optimization trajectories often require restrictive learning-rate schedules or continuously injected noise. This paper develops PAC-Bayesian analyses using specially constructed priors to obtain bounds for several gradient-based methods.

For Floored GD, a version of gradient descent with a specified precision level, the authors introduce a discrete, data-dependent prior. The resulting high-probability bound depends on accumulated squared gradient differences, scaled by learning rates and precision. These differences compare gradients from all training samples with gradients from prior samples and can be much smaller than full gradient norms. The bound covers nonconvex and nonsmooth settings.

The authors report numerically favorable test-error upper bounds, including 0.037 on MNIST, and extend the technique to a variant of stochastic gradient descent. A continuous-prior construction also yields a new bound for gradient Langevin dynamics. Its accumulated trajectory term scales with inverse sample size squared, alongside a separate inverse-sample-size term.
neurips-2022-generalization-bounds-for-g.tldr: Carefully constructed PAC-Bayesian priors yield new generalization bounds based on gradient differences for several optimization methods.

paragraphs: Accurately solving the Schrödinger equation is a central challenge in computational chemistry because the problem has very high dimensionality. Deep learning combined with Monte Carlo methods offers a promising route to accurate energy estimates at a manageable computational cost. This paper introduces an architecture intended to improve both sides of that tradeoff.

The authors report energy errors 40–70% lower than previous approaches while using six times less computation. They also calculate what they describe as the most accurate published variational ground-state energies for several atoms and molecules. These findings concern the tested chemical systems and the reported comparisons, establishing new reference results for those cases.

Beyond proposing an architecture, the paper systematically separates and measures the sources of improvement. A particular focus is the amount of physical prior knowledge built into the model. The authors find that adding more such knowledge can reduce accuracy. This makes architectural assumptions an empirical design question: physically motivated structure can be useful, but increasing it does not necessarily improve the computed energies.
neurips-2022-gold-standard-solutions-to-.tldr: A new neural architecture improves quantum energy accuracy and computational cost while showing that additional physical prior knowledge can reduce accuracy.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers model interactions between image locations through self-attention. This paper asks whether convolution-based models can efficiently provide key properties associated with that mechanism: interactions that adapt to the input, span long distances, and operate at higher orders. Its answer is a new operation called Recursive Gated Convolution.

The operation combines gated convolutions with a recursive design. It extends the second-order interactions described for self-attention to arbitrary orders without significant extra computation, and supports different convolution variants. The authors use it to construct the HorNet family of visual backbones and present it as a replaceable module for both convolutional models and vision Transformers.

Across ImageNet classification, COCO detection, and ADE20K segmentation, HorNet outperforms Swin Transformers and ConvNeXt under similar overall architectures and training configurations. The authors also report favorable scaling with more data and larger models. Applying the operation to task-specific decoders improves dense prediction with less computation, suggesting that its benefits extend beyond the main visual encoder.
neurips-2022-hornet-efficient-high-order.tldr: HorNet uses recursive gated convolutions to efficiently model adaptive, long-range, higher-order visual interactions.

paragraphs: Tractable probabilistic models allow certain probability calculations to be performed exactly and efficiently. The paper studies how to improve such a model when it was trained on a small, possibly noisy dataset but additional probability estimates are available for small subsets of variables. Those estimates may come from experts or an external process.

The proposed method updates model parameters with gradient descent. Its objective balances two forms of closeness: agreement with the local estimates, measured through KL divergence, and agreement with the original model. This creates a way to incorporate supplementary information while retaining influence from the model learned from fully observed data.

Computing the necessary gradients is NP-hard for arbitrary graphical models, but the authors show that it is efficient for tractable models. Experiments produce substantially improved models even when the local estimates are inconsistent with one another. The result matters because local information need not fit together perfectly to be useful: the optimization can reconcile competing estimates within a model that still supports efficient exact inference.
neurips-2022-learning-tractable-probabil.tldr: Balancing local probability estimates against an existing tractable model improves learning even when those estimates are inconsistent.

paragraphs: Fixed-budget best-arm identification asks how to use a limited number of samples to choose the option with the largest mean outcome. Although the probability of choosing incorrectly is known to decrease exponentially with the number of rounds, the exponent determines how quickly that improvement occurs. This paper studies the optimal worst-case rate.

The authors characterize the minimax rate through an optimization over possible parameters and introduce two rates tied to lower bounds on misidentification probability. The first, R-go, is associated with a tracking algorithm that can be implemented efficiently using a neural network. The paper reports that this algorithm outperforms existing methods, but achieving its associated rate requires a nontrivial condition.

To address that condition, the authors introduce a second rate, R-go-infinity, and prove it achievable with a conceptual algorithm called delayed optimal tracking. The distinction separates an efficiently implementable proposed method with conditional rate achievability from a conceptual method establishing achievability of the second rate. Both contribute to understanding the fundamental difficulty of allocating a fixed sampling budget.
neurips-2022-minimax-optimal-algorithms-.tldr: The paper characterizes minimax error rates for fixed-budget best-arm identification and develops tracking algorithms associated with two such rates.

paragraphs: Directed graphs can contain both transitive relationships and cycles. Transitivity means that relationships can carry through intermediate vertices, while cycles create paths that return to their starting point. Learning representations that accommodate both is challenging. The paper shows that standard box embeddings have a useful bias toward transitivity but cannot model cycles.

The authors interpret box embeddings as representing a graph through intersections of learned super-graphs. Their extension adds learned binary codes that select which graphs participate in an intersection. They explore global codes, which produce a union of intersections, and codes assigned to individual vertices, which provide greater flexibility. They also investigate regularization methods.

Theoretical and empirical results show that binary code box embeddings preserve a useful transitivity bias while having enough representational capacity to model arbitrary graphs, including cyclic ones. This addresses the conflict between a helpful structural preference and an overly restrictive representation. The capacity result concerns what the model can express; the empirical results also examine the proposed constructions in practice.
neurips-2022-modeling-transitivity-and-c.tldr: Learned binary codes extend box embeddings to represent cyclic graphs while retaining a useful bias toward transitivity.

paragraphs: This paper studies differentially private k-means and k-median clustering in a massively parallel computation setting. The challenge is to obtain useful clusters while controlling privacy-related error, total computation, and the number of parallel rounds. The authors provide two algorithms with guarantees addressing all three concerns.

Both algorithms use a constant number of rounds and total work that is near-linear in the number of points and polynomial in the number of clusters. Their error guarantees combine a relative approximation with an additive term. The first offers a constant relative approximation with a smaller stated additive-error dependence. The second approaches the optimal non-private algorithm's relative performance within a factor of one plus an arbitrarily small constant, at the cost of larger polynomial additive error.

The shared framework partitions the data and reduces the full private clustering task to private clustering within each part. A new charging argument controls how additive errors accumulate across these parts. The results make explicit the tradeoff between relative solution quality and additive error while maintaining strong parallel-efficiency guarantees.
neurips-2022-near-optimal-private-and-sc.tldr: Two private parallel clustering algorithms trade relative approximation against additive error while achieving constant rounds and efficient total work.

paragraphs: Semantic code search retrieves code from a natural-language description of what it should do. Many methods compare learned representations of the query and code. The paper focuses on a weakness of this approach: longer descriptions can combine several requirements, and matching them may demand compositional or multi-step reasoning.

NS3 supplements the query with a layout of its semantic structure. That layout breaks the final matching decision into a sequence of smaller decisions, implemented through a Neural Module Network. The structure of the description therefore helps organize the reasoning used to assess code, rather than leaving the entire decision to a single comparison between representations.

The authors evaluate NS3 on Code Search Net and Code Search and Question Answering, comparing it with methods including CodeBERT, CuBERT, and GraphCodeBERT. They report higher performance on both datasets. Additional studies examine compositional queries and support the effectiveness of the modular design. The findings indicate that explicitly organizing query meaning can improve code retrieval in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2022-ns3-neuro-symbolic-semantic.tldr: NS3 uses a query's semantic structure to organize modular reasoning and improve semantic code retrieval.

paragraphs: Deep generative networks can produce complex, high-dimensional data from simple low-dimensional random inputs. The paper seeks a theoretical explanation that takes account of the manifold hypothesis: data may occupy a low-dimensional geometric structure even when each observation has many coordinates. Its analysis explicitly assumes that the target distribution is supported on such a manifold.

Under that assumption, the authors establish approximation and estimation results for deep generative networks using Wasserstein-1 loss. The approximation perspective concerns representing the target distribution, while estimation concerns learning it from data. They show that this distributional error converges to zero at a fast rate governed by intrinsic dimension rather than ambient dimension.

This distinction explains why the number of recorded coordinates need not determine the difficulty captured by the convergence rate. The theory uses the lower-dimensional structure of the data and does not require smoothness assumptions on the data distribution. Its justification for generative modeling is therefore tied to manifold support while allowing distributions without the stated smoothness restriction.
neurips-2022-on-deep-generative-models-f.tldr: For distributions supported on low-dimensional manifolds, generative-network error rates depend on intrinsic dimension without requiring distributional smoothness.

paragraphs: Matching non-rigid objects requires finding corresponding locations despite changes in shape. A deformation field describes how positions move between the objects. This paper proposes learning a reduced representation of that field, with the aim of capturing complex movement while reducing the amount of information that must be learned from supervision.

The network predicts deformation parameters at a sparse set of spatial nodes. A mesh-free approximation then reconstructs the continuous field in closed form with guaranteed smoothness. This reduces the degrees of freedom compared with representing the field through a general-purpose neural network. The representation also provides direct access to first-order derivatives, making it easier to apply regularization to the deformation.

The authors report improved data efficiency that enables learning with limited supervision, while retaining enough expressive power to capture complex deformations. Results across multiple deformable shape-matching benchmarks reach state-of-the-art performance. The approach connects representational structure to learning efficiency: sparse learned parameters and an explicit reconstruction rule jointly determine the full deformation field.
neurips-2022-reduced-representation-of-d.tldr: Learning sparse deformation parameters and reconstructing a smooth continuous field improves data efficiency for non-rigid shape matching.

paragraphs: Sparse convolutional models describe an image signal using a small number of elements from a convolutional dictionary. This gives them a principled interpretation, but such models have historically struggled to match the classification performance of empirically designed deep networks. The paper revisits whether that performance gap can be closed.

The authors construct differentiable optimization layers from convolutional sparse coding and use them as drop-in replacements for ordinary convolutional layers. This places a structured optimization problem inside the network's computation. The design brings the sparse model's interpretation into conventional network architectures while allowing the resulting layers to participate in learning.

Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet show performance as strong as conventional neural networks. The authors also draw on sparse modeling's stable-recovery property to improve robustness. By appropriately balancing sparse regularization against data reconstruction, the models can become much more robust to input corruptions and adversarial perturbations at test time. The robustness claim depends on that balance, linking the behavior of the learned model to its optimization objective.
neurips-2022-revisiting-sparse-convoluti.tldr: Sparse-coding optimization layers match conventional image-classification performance and can improve robustness through an appropriate regularization balance.

paragraphs: Knowledge-based visual question answering must use an image together with retrieved knowledge to answer a question. The paper argues that visual representation has received insufficient attention in this setting. It identifies two weaknesses: retrieval often overlooks relationships within and among object regions, and the final answering model does not make sufficient use of visual features.

REVIVE incorporates explicit object-region information in both knowledge retrieval and answer generation. Its motivation is that individual regions and their relationships carry information that whole-image features or sliding-window features may fail to use effectively. Carrying regional evidence into both stages addresses how knowledge is selected and how that knowledge is used to produce an answer.

On the OK-VQA dataset, the authors report accuracy of 58.0, exceeding the previous state of the art by a reported 3.6%. Their detailed analysis also supports the importance of regional information across different framework components. The findings show that improving the visual side of a knowledge-based system can substantially improve its answers in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2022-revive-regional-visual-repr.tldr: REVIVE improves knowledge-based visual question answering by using object-region information during both retrieval and answer generation.

paragraphs: Causal discovery uses observational data to investigate which variables influence others. Background knowledge from experiments or human expertise can help resolve uncertainty, but unobserved confounders complicate what can be established. This paper asks which causal relationships become identifiable when such hidden variables are present and additional knowledge is available.

The authors solve this identification problem for background knowledge supplied in a local form. They provide sound and complete orientation rules. Soundness means that the rules support valid causal orientations in the stated setting; completeness means that they recover the orientations identifiable within that setting. The local form of the knowledge is part of the scope of the result.

Building on these rules, the paper proposes a general active-learning framework for causal discovery with latent confounders. This connects the identification result to a learning process that can make use of additional information. Experiments validate the framework's effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution combines a characterization of what can be inferred with a framework for using that characterization during discovery.
neurips-2022-sound-and-complete-causal-i.tldr: Sound and complete rules identify causal orientations from local background knowledge despite latent confounders and support an active-learning framework.

paragraphs: Sequence models face a tradeoff between retaining detail and compressing history. Recurrent networks strongly encourage compression into a state vector, while Transformers can attend to previously computed sequence elements. The paper argues that compressed representations may generalize better by retaining reusable structure and fewer irrelevant details, although excessive compression can reduce expressiveness.

The proposed Temporal Latent Bottleneck divides computation into a slow stream and a fast stream. The recurrent slow stream compresses chunks of K time steps into a representation distributed across multiple vectors. The fast stream uses a Transformer to process each chunk while conditioning on information from the slow stream.

This arrangement aims to retain the Transformer's expressive processing while encouraging a more compressed and structured representation across time. Experiments on visual perception and sequential decision-making tasks show improved sample efficiency and generalization relative to competitive baselines. These results support the two-stream architecture in the evaluated tasks; the proposed benefit of compression remains a motivation rather than a universal guarantee that stronger compression improves generalization.
neurips-2022-temporal-latent-bottleneck-.tldr: A recurrent slow stream and Transformer fast stream combine temporal compression with expressive processing, improving results on tested sequence tasks.

paragraphs: A model trained on past data may perform worse on future data because the underlying distribution changes. Temporal shifts come with timestamps, potentially offering information about how change develops. Wild-Time examines whether existing learning approaches can use that structure to remain effective beyond the distributions on which they were trained.

The benchmark contains five datasets covering applications including drug discovery, patient prognosis, and news classification. The authors evaluate 13 approaches spanning domain generalization, continual learning, self-supervised learning, and ensembles. They also adapt several domain-generalization methods by treating different windows of time as separate domains, allowing those methods to address temporal variation.

Two protocols serve different evaluation needs. Eval-Fix uses a fixed time split as a simple primary protocol, while Eval-Stream provides a complementary streaming evaluation for continual learning. Across the studied settings, the authors observe an average performance drop of 20% from in-distribution to out-of-distribution data. The benchmark therefore exposes substantial remaining difficulty in handling real temporal change, even with methods intended to address distribution shifts.
neurips-2022-wild-time-a-benchmark-of-in.tldr: Wild-Time benchmarks real temporal distribution shifts and finds substantial performance degradation across existing approaches.
